name: DevOps Interview Prep
subject: devops
description: CI/CD, Docker, Kubernetes, infrastructure as code, and SRE fundamentals

questions.question: What is the key difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?
options: Images are running; containers are stopped
An image is a read-only template; a container is a running instance of an image
Containers are stored in a registry; images run on a host
There is no difference
questions.explanation: An image is a static, read-only blueprint. A container is a live, isolated process created from an image.

questions.question: What does 'Infrastructure as Code' (IaC) mean?
options: Writing code that runs on infrastructure
Managing and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable config files instead of manual processes
Building infrastructure components from scratch in code
Converting physical servers to virtual machines
questions.explanation: IaC (Terraform, Pulumi, AWS CloudFormation) describes infrastructure in version-controlled files, enabling repeatable, auditable provisioning.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a CI/CD pipeline?
options: Compiling code only
Automating build, test, and deployment steps so code changes reach production reliably and quickly
Monitoring production applications
Managing user authentication
questions.explanation: CI (Continuous Integration) automates build+test on every commit. CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment) automates releasing to production.

questions.question: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?
options: Horizontal = add more resources to existing machine; Vertical = add more machines
Horizontal = add more machines; Vertical = add more resources to existing machine
Horizontal is for databases; Vertical is for web servers
They are the same thing
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling (scale out): add more servers. Vertical scaling (scale up): increase RAM/CPU on existing server.

questions.question: What does a Kubernetes Deployment's 'replicas' field control?
options: Number of containers per pod
Number of pod instances running at any time
Number of nodes in the cluster
Maximum CPU allowed per pod
questions.explanation: replicas: 3 means Kubernetes keeps 3 identical pod instances running. If one dies, it's automatically replaced.

questions.question: What is the difference between blue-green and canary deployments?
options: Blue-green uses two environments with full traffic switch; canary gradually shifts a percentage of traffic
Blue-green is for databases; canary is for web servers
Canary uses two environments; blue-green gradually shifts traffic
They are identical strategies
questions.explanation: Blue-green: two identical environments, instant full cutover. Canary: slowly increase traffic to new version while monitoring.

questions.question: What does SLO (Service Level Objective) define?
options: A legal commitment to customers
A target reliability goal (e.g., 99.9% uptime) for a service
The maximum number of requests per second
The on-call escalation policy
questions.explanation: SLO is the target value for an SLI (e.g., 99.9% availability). SLA is the contractual version with penalties for breach.

questions.question: What is Terraform's 'plan' command used for?
options: Applies infrastructure changes immediately
Shows what changes will be made without applying them
Initializes Terraform providers
Destroys all infrastructure
questions.explanation: terraform plan generates an execution plan showing what Terraform will create, modify, or destroy — without making any changes.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of using a container orchestrator like Kubernetes?
options: Containers run faster with orchestration
Automatically manages scheduling, scaling, healing, and networking of containers across a cluster
Provides a GUI for container management
Eliminates the need for Docker images
questions.explanation: Kubernetes automates deployment, scaling, self-healing (restarts failed pods), and service discovery across many hosts.

questions.question: What does 'git rebase' do compared to 'git merge'?
options: Rebase merges branches; merge doesn't
Rebase replays commits on top of another branch for a linear history; merge creates a merge commit
They are identical
Rebase deletes branches; merge preserves them
questions.explanation: rebase moves/replays commits onto a new base, creating a cleaner linear history. merge preserves the branch topology with a merge commit.

questions.question: What is an error budget in SRE?
options: Budget allocated for fixing production bugs
The allowed amount of downtime/unreliability defined by (100% - SLO)
The maximum number of on-call incidents per month
The cost allowed for infrastructure errors
questions.explanation: Error budget = 100% - SLO. A 99.9% SLO allows 0.1% downtime (~8.7 hours/year). Burning the budget fast slows new feature releases.

questions.question: What does a Dockerfile's ENTRYPOINT instruction do?
options: Specifies the base image
Sets the working directory inside the container
Defines the executable that runs when the container starts
Exposes a port on the container
questions.explanation: ENTRYPOINT sets the primary command that runs when the container starts. CMD provides default arguments to ENTRYPOINT.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of Prometheus in a DevOps stack?
options: Log aggregation and search
Time-series metrics collection and alerting
Distributed tracing
Container image registry
questions.explanation: Prometheus scrapes metrics from endpoints, stores them as time-series, and triggers alerts via Alertmanager. Grafana visualizes the data.

questions.question: What is GitOps?
options: Using Git for code review only
Using Git as the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and application state
Running git commands in CI pipelines
Automating Git branch creation
questions.explanation: GitOps uses Git PRs as the operational mechanism — infrastructure changes are applied by reconciling the cluster state with the desired state in Git.

questions.question: What is a service mesh (e.g., Istio, Linkerd) responsible for?
options: Managing Kubernetes node pools
Handling service-to-service communication — mTLS, retries, circuit breaking, observability
Providing persistent storage to services
Load balancing external traffic only
questions.explanation: A service mesh adds a sidecar proxy to each pod, handling cross-cutting concerns like mutual TLS, load balancing, retries, and distributed tracing.
